素.shuowen: 白緻繒也。从糸、𠂹，取其澤也。
素.shuowenEn: White, close-woven silk. From 糸 (silk) and 𠂹 (to hang down); chosen for its sheen.

parts.m: top: the Shuowen’s 𠂹, a thing that hangs

素.story: Silk cloth as it leaves the loom, before any dye. Thinkers of every school used it as the image of what a person is before teaching and habit colour them. The Laozi says it once: 見素抱樸, “show the undyed silk, hold the uncarved wood” (19). The Shuowen defines 樸, the wood, as 木素: the 素 of wood. Together the two became the ordinary word 樸素, plain.
素.gap: “Purity” is a moral word with dirt as its opposite. 素 has no dirt in view. Its opposite is colour and pattern.

棄.shuowen: 捐也。从廾推𠦒棄之，从𠫓。𠫓，逆子也。
棄.shuowenEn: To cast off. From two hands (廾) that push a winnowing basket (𠦒) to throw a thing out, and from 𠫓. 𠫓 is a child reversed.

parts.m: a child, head down: a new-born

棄.story: The graph shows a new-born carried out in a basket. The ancestor of the Zhou house, Lord Millet, was named 棄 because his mother exposed him three times. In the Laozi the word is used with force: throw away cleverness, right conduct, profit (19). And with tenderness: the sage is good at saving people, so no person is 棄; good at saving things, so no thing is 棄 (27).
棄.gap: “Discard” is light. 棄 is what one does to a thing that was one’s own.

盜.shuowen: 私利物也。从㳄，㳄欲皿者。
盜.shuowenEn: To make a thing one’s private gain. From 㳄 (spittle): one who drools with desire for the dish (皿).
盜.story: A wet mouth over someone else’s dish. The Laozi treats robbery as a product of government and fashion. Do not prize rare goods and the people will not rob (3); throw away skill and profit and there are no robbers (19); the court is splendid and the fields are weeds: this is called the boast of robbers (53); the more laws are published, the more robbers there are (57).
盜.gap: English “thief” blames a person. The graph and the book both look first at the dish, and at who made it so desirable.

senses: to sever, to break off; to end
絕.shuowenEn: To cut silk thread. From 糸 (silk), 刀 (knife), and 卩.
絕.story: A knife on a thread: a continuous thing is ended at one stroke. The three bans of passage 19 use it, and so does the line that follows them, 絕學無憂, “cut off learning: no worry” (20).
絕.gap: “Renounce” happens in the conscience. 絕 happens under a blade.

senses: crossed lines; a pattern; a tattoo
a written graph; writing; a text
文.shuowenEn: Crossed strokes. It pictures a crossing pattern.
文.story: First a pattern of lines, on cloth, on bronze, or on skin; the early graph is commonly explained as a person with a mark on the chest. Then all that is patterned in human life: writing, literature, manners, culture. For Confucians it was the precious inheritance of Zhou. The Laozi uses it rarely and coolly: the three bans, “as 文”, are not enough (19); those who wear 文 and coloured silks while the fields are bare are robbers (53).
文.gap: English splits it into “pattern”, “text”, “culture”, and “civil”. In Chinese the weave of a cloth and the classics of a people are one word.

巧.shuowenEn: Technique. From 工 (work; a carpenter’s square), with 丂 for the sound.
巧.story: The craftsman’s gift, and the cunning that grows from it. Passage 19 says to cut it off; passage 45 says 大巧若拙, “great skill seems clumsy”; passage 57 says that the more skills people have, the more strange things appear.
巧.gap: “Skill” is praise in English. 巧 has a shadow: too clever by half.

senses: 寡人: “the lonely one”, a ruler’s word for himself
寡.shuowen: 少也。从宀从頒。頒，分賦也，故爲少。
寡.shuowenEn: Few. From 宀 (roof) and 頒. 頒 is to share out, and so there is little.
寡.story: Few, and so alone. Kings called themselves 寡人, and the Laozi notes it twice: lords and kings name themselves “orphaned, lonely, without grain” (39, 42). As a verb it is “to reduce”: 寡欲, fewer wants (19); 小國寡民, a small state with few people (80).
寡.gap: 寡欲 is often turned into “desireless”. It says “few”.

senses: to belong to; a kind, a class
zhǔ: to attach; to entrust, to enjoin
屬.shuowenEn: To connect. From 尾 (tail), with 蜀 for the sound.
屬.story: What follows on behind and is joined, as a tail to a body. In passage 19 the bare bans are given “something to belong to”: plain silk and uncarved wood.
屬.gap: English must choose “belong”, “attach”, or “entrust”. The picture is a thing that hangs on to another.
